mcq.q: Which number best ties AI spend to value?
options: Total monthly invoice
Cost per GPU-hour
Cost per input token
Cost per successful task
mcq.why: It includes failures and people and divides by what was achieved.

mcq.q: A request costs 0.017 dollars, 15% fail and each failure costs 1.20 dollars of agent time; 85% succeed. Cost per success is about…
options: 0.02 dollars
0.23 dollars
0.20 dollars
1.20 dollars

mcq.q: Output tokens cost 15 and input 3 dollars per million. 350 output tokens cost about…
options: 0.00053 dollars
0.0053 dollars
0.0011 dollars
0.053 dollars

mcq.q: Most of a support feature’s cost per success is people fixing failures. The best lever is usually…
options: Shortening the system prompt
Turning off prompt caching
Switching to a cheaper model
Raising the success rate
mcq.why: Each avoided failure saves far more than its tokens.
distractors: Small saving on a minor line.
May lower success and raise people cost.

mcq.q: Why keep a versioned price table with usage records?
options: So the provider can bill you a second time
So past costs can be recomputed after price changes
Because tokens change size from month to month
So prompts can stay in the cache for longer
mcq.why: Cost history stays explainable when prices change.
distractors: Token counts are what they are.

mcq.q: Retries run at 5%. The model cost line should be multiplied by…
mcq.why: Each retry is another paid call: 1 + 0.05.

mcq.q: A team reports only total monthly spend. Agent steps per task double; what will they see first?
options: Nothing until users complain
An alert on cost per task
A drop in answer quality
A bill rising for no visible reason
mcq.why: Without unit costs, the cause hides in the total.

mcq.q: Which cost line is most often forgotten?
options: The embedding model calls
Input tokens from the prompt
Output tokens from the model
People reviewing or fixing outputs
mcq.why: Human time rarely appears in the AI bill but often dominates.

mcq.q: Unit cost is 0.02 dollars per request and a sale month brings 40 times the usual 3 million requests. The sale-month model bill is about…
options: 240,000 dollars
2.4 million dollars
24,000 dollars
60,000 dollars

mcq.q: Which data must every usage record carry to build unit costs?
options: Tokens, model, feature, tenant and outcome
Only the total number of tokens in the month
The model’s full answer text, word for word
The user’s full message text, word for word
mcq.why: Tags and outcome let cost be split and divided by successes.

mcq.q: Why does putting the current date at the start of the prompt hurt cost?
options: Dates use more tokens than other words
It breaks prefix caching for everything after it
Providers charge extra for dates
It forces a larger model to be used
mcq.why: A changing prefix means no cache hits.
distractors: A date is a few tokens.

mcq.q: Cutting answers from 500 to 300 tokens at 15 dollars per million output tokens over 3 million requests saves…
options: 900 dollars a month
9,000 dollars a month
1,800 dollars a month
90,000 dollars a month

mcq.q: Which saving should be checked most carefully against quality?
options: Using the batch interface
Caching stable instructions
Retrieving fewer chunks
Moving the date after the instructions
mcq.why: Fewer chunks can drop the evidence an answer needs.

mcq.q: Caching 2,160 instruction tokens moves them from 3 to 0.30 dollars per million. Over 3 million requests the saving is about…
options: 17,500 dollars
1,750 dollars
6,500 dollars
19,400 dollars
distractors: Uses the full price, not the difference.

mcq.q: After trimming instructions, one rule the model needed was lost. How should that be caught?
options: A regression suite run after each cut
A check of the monthly invoice
A look at the new token count
Asking the model if anything is missing
mcq.why: Quality checks after every change catch dropped behaviour.

mcq.q: Why do output tokens deserve attention first in many features?
options: They cannot be cached by providers
They usually cost several times more per token
They are billed even when not shown
They are always more numerous than input
mcq.why: Higher per-token prices make output the biggest lever.
distractors: True but not the main reason.

mcq.q: A long chat sends every past turn with each request. A safe reduction is…
options: Drop all of the history after five turns
Send only the last word the user typed
Stop the chat entirely after ten turns
Summarise older turns, keep key facts verbatim
mcq.why: Summaries keep context; key identifiers must survive exactly (7.5).

mcq.q: Reranking 20 candidates and keeping the top 4 instead of sending 8 unranked chunks mainly…
options: Raises tokens because a reranker is added
Cuts tokens while keeping the best evidence
Makes prompt caching impossible to use
Removes the need for any retrieval step
mcq.why: Better ordering lets you send fewer chunks.
distractors: The reranker’s cost is small next to tokens saved.

mcq.q: Cutting 200 input tokens at 3 dollars per million over 3 million requests saves…
options: 18,000 dollars
9,000 dollars
1,800 dollars
180 dollars

mcq.q: A format instruction "answer in at most three sentences" halves output length but two slices fail. What next?
options: Raise the temperature to compensate
Remove the limit for all requests
Keep it everywhere; average is fine
Keep the limit except for those slices
mcq.why: Apply savings where quality holds; exempt slices that need length.

interview.q: What levers reduce tokens in an LLM feature?
How does prompt caching work and how do you get high hit rates?
Why must every token cut be followed by an evaluation?
Answers got longer after a model upgrade and the bill rose. What do you do?
interview.followUp: How do you prevent it next time?

interview.q: How do you reduce cost in long multi-turn chats?
interview.followUp: Which facts must never be summarised away?

interview.q: Your cache hit rate is near zero. How do you investigate?
interview.followUp: How do you measure the hit rate?

interview.q: Design a token budget for a RAG feature at three million requests a month.
How would you run a cost-reduction programme across many prompts?
interview.followUp: How do you report savings honestly?

mcq.q: Which work suits a 24-hour batch interface?
options: Live chat answers
A user waiting for a rebooking
Fraud checks during payment
Weekly evaluation runs
mcq.why: No one is waiting and the deadline is days.

mcq.q: Re-embedding 1 billion tokens at 4 dollars per million costs 4,000. At half price in batch it costs…
options: 400 dollars
4,000 dollars
2,000 dollars
1,000 dollars

mcq.q: A digest is needed by 08:00 and the batch window is 24 hours. The safe choice is…
options: Submit it to the batch interface at 07:00
Run it on idle GPUs overnight or real-time
Skip the digest on the busiest days
Submit it to the batch interface at 01:00
mcq.why: A 24-hour window can deliver after 08:00; use your own off-peak capacity.

mcq.q: Why are self-hosted GPUs often cheap for night work?
options: Providers give discounts for night-time usage
Electricity for servers is free at night
They are sized for the day and idle at night
Requests at night use fewer tokens each
mcq.why: The capacity is already paid for; using it raises utilisation.
distractors: Tokens do not depend on time.

mcq.q: Jobs totalling 61,520 dollars a month save 3,160 in batch. The saving is about…
distractors: That is the discount, not the share.

mcq.q: Why match batch outputs to inputs by an id you assign?
options: Without an id the outputs are never saved
Results may return out of order or partly fail
Adding ids makes the batch run much faster
The provider needs the ids for its billing
mcq.why: Ids let you reconcile and retry failures.

mcq.q: A bank batches dispute letters with a legal deadline in 48 hours. The risk is…
options: Batch results cannot be audited afterwards
The batch quietly uses a different model
A delayed batch pushes letters past the deadline
Letters come back shorter when run in batch
mcq.why: Regulated deadlines need guaranteed timing.

mcq.q: Live chat is 78% of a bill and cannot be batched. Batch work is 22% and gets 50% off. The best total saving is…
What should happen to items that fail inside a batch job?
options: Resubmit them and record the failures
Send them to live chat users
Rerun the whole batch from scratch
Ignore them; batches are best effort
mcq.why: Retry the failed items only and keep counts.

mcq.q: Which statement about batch pricing is safest?
options: Every provider gives exactly 50% off
Batch results always arrive within an hour
Batch is only for embedding models
Discounts and windows vary by provider; check terms
mcq.why: Terms differ; the course uses illustrative figures.
distractors: Windows are often up to 24 hours.
Also for chat and other models.

interview.q: Which AI workloads can move to batch or off-peak?
How does a batch interface work?
interview.followUp: How do you handle partial failure?

interview.q: Why use idle self-hosted capacity at night?
A nightly job sometimes finishes after the team needs it. What do you change?
interview.followUp: How do you guarantee the time?

interview.q: Which jobs in a regulated workflow should never be batched?
How would you estimate the saving from moving work to batch?
interview.followUp: How do you check the estimate after a month?

interview.q: Design the scheduling of bulk AI work for a company with its own GPU cluster.
interview.followUp: How do you stop bulk work hurting daytime traffic?

interview.q: Design a monthly re-embedding of a large corpus at the lowest cost.
interview.followUp: How do you avoid re-embedding unchanged documents?

mcq.q: Cost-aware routing chooses a model by…
options: Whichever model happened to answer last
Request type and its measured quality bar
The time of day the request arrived
How fast the user typed the request
mcq.why: Each type goes to the cheapest model that met the bar in evaluation.

mcq.q: 1,000 requests: 400 small at 0.0002, 450 mid at 0.0015, 150 large at 0.006. Total cost is…
options: 2.55 dollars
0.98 dollars
6.00 dollars
1.655 dollars

mcq.q: How does routing differ from a cascade?
options: They are two names for the same thing
Routing always sends work to the largest model
Routing decides up front; a cascade tries small first
A cascade never escalates any requests
mcq.why: Routing uses the request type; a cascade reacts to the small model’s result.

mcq.q: Fallbacks from the small model rise from 3% to 15% for one type. This suggests…
options: The small model no longer meets the bar for it
The large model has become cheaper
Traffic has dropped for that type
The gateway is mislabelling every type
mcq.why: A rising fallback rate is a quality signal for that route.

mcq.q: The quality bar is raised from 90% to 94%. Expect…
options: Lower overall cost
Fewer types on larger models
More types routed to larger models
No change in the routing table
mcq.why: Fewer cheap models meet a higher bar.
distractors: The table depends on the bar.

mcq.q: Why evaluate per request type rather than overall?
options: Request types are easier to label by hand
Overall scores are always lower than per type
Providers require per-type evaluation
A model can pass overall and fail one type
mcq.why: Averages hide types where the cheap model fails.

mcq.q: Everything on the large model costs 6 dollars per 1,000 requests; routed, 1.66. The saving is about…
A security report is cheap to route to a small model, which scored 91%. The routing rule should…
options: Send security reports to the strongest model
Drop security reports from routing
Use the small model since 91% passes
Pick a model at random each time
mcq.why: High-stakes types override cost.
distractors: Cost should not decide high-stakes routes.

mcq.q: 5% of 400 small-model answers fall back to the large model at 0.006 dollars. The extra cost is…
options: 0.024 dollars
0.12 dollars
1.20 dollars
0.012 dollars

mcq.q: When a provider releases a new model, the routing table should…
options: Send everything to the new model
Stay unchanged
Be replaced by a cascade
Be re-evaluated per type
mcq.why: Model changes alter who meets the bar (18.5).

How do you build a routing table?
interview.followUp: How often do you rebuild it?

interview.q: Routing or cascade: when would you choose each?
Fallbacks for one route are rising. What do you do?
How do you keep high-stakes requests away from cheap models?
interview.followUp: How do you detect a misclassified high-stakes request?

interview.q: How do you add language to a routing table?
interview.followUp: What if a language has little data?

Plan how routing tables stay correct as models and traffic change.

mcq.q: Showback means…
options: Blocking each team once it reaches its limit
Reporting each team’s spend without moving money
Moving spend into each team’s own budget
Refunding each team’s unused spend
mcq.why: It shows usage; chargeback moves the money.

mcq.q: Shared costs of 2,000 split by usage; team A used 4,000 of 8,000 direct spend. A’s share is…
options: 1,000 dollars
667 dollars
2,000 dollars
500 dollars

mcq.q: A team has used 5,000 of a 6,000 budget. Which alert has fired?
options: None
50% only

mcq.q: Untagged spend keeps growing. The best fix is…
options: Refuse untagged calls at the gateway
Split untagged spend evenly each month
Ignore it below 20% of the bill
Ask teams to tag voluntarily
mcq.why: Enforcement at one choke point works; goodwill does not.

mcq.q: Why start with showback before chargeback?
options: Chargeback needs no tagging
Showback is more accurate
Chargeback is illegal in most places
Teams must trust the numbers first
mcq.why: Moving money on disputed numbers causes conflict.

mcq.q: A regulated dispute process hits its budget. The right policy is…
options: Block it until next month
Switch it to the cheapest model
Remove its budget entirely
Alert and review; do not block it
mcq.why: Blocking would breach service commitments; soft limits fit.

mcq.q: Spend is 4,000, 3,000 and 1,000 with 2,000 shared split by usage. Team C’s total is…
options: 1,250 dollars
1,667 dollars
3,000 dollars
1,000 dollars

mcq.q: Which allocation key is usually fairest for a shared vector database?
options: An equal split between all the teams
Alphabetical order of the team names
Each team’s share of queries or stored vectors
The number of people in each team
mcq.why: Usage-based keys reflect who drives the cost.

mcq.q: Showback reveals one tool calls the assistant on every page load. The likely next step is…
options: Switch the whole company to a cheaper model
Raise the team’s budget to fit
Fix the integration and add a per-team limit
Hide the tool from the report
mcq.why: Fix the cause and add a guard.

mcq.q: Which limit suits an experiment with an external API key?
options: A limit set after the first bill
A hard limit that blocks at the budget
A soft limit with monthly review
No limit during the experiment
mcq.why: Experiments can run away; block at the cap.

interview.q: Explain showback and chargeback.
How do you allocate shared AI platform costs?
interview.followUp: What if teams dispute the key?

A team says showback numbers are wrong. How do you respond?
How do you set budgets for regulated processes?

mcq.q: Committed spend gives a lower unit price in exchange for…
options: Guaranteed access to all future models
Free usage above the commitment
A promise to never change providers
Paying for the committed amount even if unused
mcq.why: You pay for the commitment whether or not you use it.

mcq.q: Forecast is 100 units a month, give or take 25. A sensible commitment is…
options: About 85, below the forecast
Exactly 100, the forecast
125, the high case
Zero, to stay flexible
mcq.why: Commit to what you are confident of; burst on demand.

mcq.q: Committed units cost 0.70 and on-demand 1.00. In a month using 60 of 100 committed units you pay…
options: 70, against 60 on demand
100, against 60 on demand
42, against 60 on demand
60, against 70 on demand

mcq.q: On-demand prices fall 40% mid-year to 0.60, below the committed 0.70. A long commitment then…
options: Becomes free for the rest of the year
Costs more than not committing
Is automatically renegotiated
Still saves 30% as before
mcq.why: The committed rate is now higher than on demand.
distractors: The discount was against the old price.

mcq.q: Which clause protects you when models are retired?
options: An exit fee paid to the provider on leaving
A longer term at the same unit price
A higher committed amount each month
The right to move the commitment to newer models
mcq.why: Model-swap rights keep the commitment usable (18.5).

mcq.q: Why are commitments riskier for AI than for ordinary servers?
options: Providers do not offer discounts
Prices and models change quickly
Tokens cannot be forecast at all
AI usage never changes
mcq.why: Fast price drops and deprecations make long terms risky.
distractors: They can be forecast with ranges.

mcq.q: A store with sale peaks of forty times normal should commit to…
options: The everyday base load only
Nothing, buying all on demand
The peak sale volume
The average including sales
mcq.why: Base load is used every month; peaks are short.

mcq.q: Reserved GPU capacity mainly guarantees…
options: Capacity is available when you need it
Higher model accuracy
Lower prices than any provider API
Freedom from operations work
mcq.why: Reservations secure capacity, useful for known peaks.

mcq.q: Commit 85 at 0.70 and use 110 at 1.00 on demand above it. The month costs…
Which terms belong in the same negotiation as price?
options: Only the length of the contract term
Only the discount percentage on offer
Only the support phone number and hours
Data handling, residency and price-drop protection
mcq.why: Changing provider later is costly; agree the whole package (16.5).
